statement: A single LB server becomes a bottleneck: for every client request it receives it must open another TCP connection to a backend server, so with a 10,000 TCP connection limit it can serve at most 5,000 concurrent clients.
detail: Half of the connection budget is consumed by the connections from the LB server to the backend servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the maximum number of concurrent TCP connection or maximum number of client that it can serve is only 5000

statement: Because one LB machine is a bottleneck, the LB servers themselves need to be horizontally scaled; the brainstorm also covers how load balancers are internally scaled.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So which means that this needs to be horizontally scaling.

statement: The load balancer design brainstorm touches four factors: LB configurations, monitoring, availability and extensibility.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the four factors that we would brainstorm on is LB configurations, monitoring, availability and extensibility

statement: The LB configuration must store the IP address and port of every backend server connected to the load balancer.
detail: Proposed by a student (Student 6) as 'backend server configurations, IP address'; the teacher accepted and refined it to an IP address and port mapping.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: All the backend servers that you have, you would have IP address and port mapping of all of them.

statement: The bare-minimum LB configuration is the load balancing algorithm in use plus the list of backend servers; the system can be made infinitely more complex with fancier stuff, but the design starts from the bare minimum.
detail: The balancing algorithm was suggested by a student (Student 6); the teacher accepted it.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: this is the bare minimum that you need, that what algorithm you are using and what are the backend servers that are connected to that

statement: The LB configuration can be stored in a database, as the simple starting point.
detail: Student 6's proposal; the teacher kept the database but pointed out (using the student's own remark) that reading it on every request is painful.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: If I go from the beginning, let's think about the simple system. I will just use a database for that.

statement: A load balancer should add as little latency as possible; if the LB server called the database for the configuration on every request, every request would take longer.
detail: Raised by Student 6 and endorsed by the teacher: the load balancer already adds a network hop, and a DB call per request on top of that just slows things down.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So you want this to be bare minimum.

statement: A network call to the database costs about three to five milliseconds, which is too expensive to pay on every request passing through the load balancer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: And this network call itself is very expensive, three milliseconds to five milliseconds.

statement: When an LB server starts it pulls the configuration of its load balancer from the database and keeps an in-memory copy, so incoming requests are routed without any network call.
detail: Student 6 proposed pulling at startup or polling the DB at intervals; the teacher restated it as an in-memory copy loaded at startup.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: keep an in-memory copy so that when the request comes in, you don't have to make a network call

statement: In the demo load balancer code the configuration is just a simple in-memory list of backends; the LB picks one from it at random or according to the balancing strategy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In the demo, right, you have a simple list

statement: An in-memory copy of the configuration goes out of sync when the configuration changes, for example when a backend server goes down, so something must keep the LB servers updated.
detail: Student 6 raised it in answer to the teacher's question about the disadvantage of the in-memory copy; the teacher took it up.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So we need something which like keep on updating the server.

statement: Before updating anything, the system must first detect that a backend server went down; this needs a health check service that keeps checking the backend servers.
detail: Proposed by Student 6; the teacher was delighted ('exactly taking it in the direction I wanted it to go').
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: there should be some health check service. Like I should keep on sending the details of the server.

statement: The component that performs health checks on the backend servers is called the orchestrator; it is the 'mastermind' of the load balancer system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: that I always used for orchestrator
flags: check: phrase sounds garbled - possibly "fancy word that I always use"

statement: A backend server is considered up if its dedicated health check endpoint (not all user requests) returns HTTP 200.
detail: Student 6 first said the server responding 200; the teacher asked whether that meant all user requests, and the student clarified it is only for the health endpoint. The teacher accepted: health check endpoint, implemented however you like.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: if it is sending the response 200, then I can think of like it's working properly

statement: A student suggested that no specialized health check endpoint is needed: a very lightweight endpoint that just responds to a ping, or TCP pings to the port and IP to see if any packet comes back.
detail: The teacher's only direct reply was to ask whether the student had ever configured a load balancer; he then explained why an explicit health check endpoint configured on the load balancer is used.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we don't necessarily need to have a specialized health check endpoint

statement: A backend server is a virtual machine that may run hundreds of processes (SSH, nginx, other HTTP servers), but for the load balancer only one process matters: the core web server it balances against, e.g. the profile service on port 8081.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: with respect to this load balancer, there is one process that matters

statement: Every HTTP server you build should define a health check endpoint such as /status or /health.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: on every HTTP server that we create, we always have some health check, let's say slash status or slash

statement: The health check endpoint is part of the load balancer configuration: apart from the load balancing algorithm, you provide the health check endpoint when you spin up a load balancer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you typically configure this endpoint on the load balancer site, which tells you that this is my health check endpoint

statement: Checking that the VM is up is not enough: the VM can be up while the service process crashed (e.g. a divide-by-zero or null pointer exception), and then it cannot serve requests; the health check must verify the service, not the server.
detail: The orchestrator could check the VM through its infrastructure access, but that misses a crashed process.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we just don't need that VM to be up, but we need our process to be up
flags: check: sentence cut off between 01:18:03 and 01:18:09

statement: The orchestrator uses the health check configuration to fire continuous health checks at the backend servers; typically it makes HTTP calls to each server and needs a 200 response.
detail: Other protocols are also accepted; HTTP is a simplification.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Typically orchestrator itself makes those HTTP calls to each of the servers and needs to get a 200 response.

statement: The orchestrator needs access to the configuration database to know the servers and their health check endpoint; when a health check fails it immediately updates the database, removing the dead backend's entry.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When one of the server is down, the health check would fail. Orchestrator would immediately go and update the database.

statement: The key problem: how does a change the orchestrator makes in the database reach the in-memory hash map of configuration held by every LB server?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: how would this change that orchestrator made in the DB get updated in the LB servers in memory, in-memory hash map that it has?

statement: The most naive way to propagate config changes is for each LB server to keep polling the database, which is not optimal.
detail: The student (Student 7) first argued polling hurts because the process checks backend liveness while serving requests; the teacher corrected that the orchestrator does the health checks, so user requests on the LB server are unaffected by them. The real problem with polling is staleness (next item).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: the most naive way would be for the LB server to keep pulling, but that would not be an optimal way
flags: check: speaker of 01:20:46 - transcript labels both Anubhav and Anwar as Student 7

statement: Instead of polling, an event-based solution could have the database communicate the change, triggered whenever the change happens.
detail: The teacher: 'So you reached that point'.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Instead of polling, like if there was a way for the database to communicate it to...
flags: check: "Got it." may be Teacher (speaker map: check context)

statement: Polling has a frequency, say 10 seconds: if a backend crashes at the first second of a polling interval, for the remaining nine (N minus one) seconds requests keep going to the dead backend server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: for nine seconds your request will still continue to go to backend server. Even though that's dead.

statement: Because the LB server routes from its in-memory configuration and does not check the DB per request, a stale configuration means user requests fail for that whole window, a spike in error rate for end users; this is the main reason polling cannot be used.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you still have your user request not being handled successfully, which is spike in error rate for your end user.

statement: Push-based config update: reserve a separate port on the LB server for updating configuration; whoever detects a change (e.g. the orchestrator) calls that endpoint, and the LB server then pulls the new configuration from the DB.
detail: Proposed by a student (Student 4); the teacher called it a push-based mechanism and 'a good one'.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: If there is a change in configuration, we can just call LB to update that configuration instead of like polling.

statement: A student proposed a separate 'load balancer handler' service to watch for configuration changes; the teacher rejected adding one more service: let the orchestrator (or the LB server itself) do it.
detail: Teacher: 'Why I have one more service to do that.' The student then simplified: the orchestrator updates the DB and calls the load balancer to pull from the DB.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: We can, we can have some kind of load balancer handler

statement: Configuration changes come not only from health checks but also from developers through LB console APIs (e.g. in the AWS console explicitly adding backend servers, changing the balancing algorithm or health check); every such change goes to the database and must reach the LB servers' in-memory copy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: any change in configuration by any developer, adding more backend servers, changing load balancing algorithm, changing health check status

statement: With the push-based approach, whoever changes the configuration calls the LB server's other port and asks it to pull from the DB, which is near immediate.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This would be near immediate.

statement: There is no one right answer in design: everything is a trade-off; the student's push approach works in some situations and the teacher's in others.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because everything is a trade-off, right?

statement: Concretely, the LB server runs its main process on port 9090 plus one more process on port 9091 (a 'meta' port); anyone changing the configuration makes a normal call to this port, and its handler reads the DB and updates the in-memory configuration.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: apart from that have one more process which is running on port 9091

statement: Polling fails because the LB may keep operating on stale data; the goal is (almost) zero staleness, so every change must be pushed out immediately.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We want zero staleness, almost zero staleness.

statement: The same problem appeared in the previous session's design of Slack's real-time communication: polling could not be relied on and things had to be pushed immediately; the same idea (listening for changes, as with membership information there) applies to LB config.
case_study: Reuses the Slack real-time messaging design from the previous session.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when we designed Slack's real-time communication, we saw this very problem that we could not rely on polling

statement: One implementation (not the only one) is a real-time Pub/Sub such as Redis: whenever the configuration in the DB changes, a message is pushed to the broker (e.g. via CDC) and the LB servers listen to it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you can have a real-time Pub/Sub like Redis, whose job is that whenever you update something in the DB, it pushes a message via CDC

statement: CDC (change data capture) is only sprinkled in here as a sneak peek; it is covered in depth in the fifth week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll talk about CDC in depth in fifth week

statement: The message to the broker can be published by the orchestrator, directly by the LB console, or by the database through CDC.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: either your orchestrator can do this part, your LB console can also directly push message to broker, or your database using CDC

statement: Make systems reactive rather than polling-based to minimize staleness; on an event the LB server either uses the pushed config or pulls the latest config from the DB, an implementation choice.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We need to make things reactive rather than polling based.

statement: Two reactive approaches were discussed: an explicit API call asking the LB server to pull the config, or a reactive Pub/Sub mechanism that pushes the configuration; either way the LB server updates its in-memory copy (via shared memory between its processes), and which works depends on the case.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One using an explicit API call that ask it to pull it.

statement: Besides the backend servers, someone must keep an eye on the LB servers too; the orchestrator does this, and 'keeping an eye' means not only health but whether the server is overwhelmed (CPU, memory and so on).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is also a need for someone to keep an eye on this LB servers also
flags: check: sentence cut off, possible lost speech before 01:30:31

statement: If the orchestrator sees very high CPU on the LB servers it adds one more LB server, and removes one when the load drops; one LB server is definitely not enough, LB servers must scale horizontally.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if it sees very high CPU consumption, it might just want to add one more LB server into the system

statement: To make scaling decisions the orchestrator needs the key vitals of each LB server: CPU, memory, network and disk.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: CPU, memory, network, disk, everything, those key vitals of your LB server

statement: A student proposed that the orchestrator periodically make status/health-check API calls to each LB server to get its current CPU, memory and disk utilization; the teacher called this unrealistic because a point-in-time reading is not enough.
detail: Correction: the orchestrator needs historical data, e.g. to see that CPU utilization is rising and act; it needs a generic way, not just orchestrator and LB talking to each other.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I think normal status and health checks that we discussed about between orchestrator and

statement: Scaling decisions need historical metric data, not just the current value, so that a rising trend can be acted on.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What if it needs historical data?

statement: Do not limit monitoring to the orchestrator and the load balancer: you want to see overall infrastructure utilization and historical trends, so the data must be stored somewhere.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: won't you want to see overall infrastructure utilization, historical trends and whatnot

statement: Metrics should not go into the same database as the configuration: the configuration store is key-value data, while CPU, memory, disk and network utilization is time series data.
detail: A student (Student 3) proposed reusing the configuration database; the teacher corrected that this is time series data, unlike the key-value configuration.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: What you're storing is time series data, CPU utilization, memory, disk network.

statement: Asking a server for its utilization only at the moment is too late: a server at 100% utilization may not even respond, leaving no time to react; you want to react at 60, 70, 80% and need historical trends such as average utilization.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You'd want to react when it is like 60, 70, 80%.

statement: A student proposed that the orchestrator keep its own database fed by heartbeat messages from the load balancer reporting CPU utilization; the teacher rejected re-implementing something other systems already do.
detail: Teacher: 'Why are you re-implementing things that are already implemented by other systems? Just reuse the stuff.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Orchestrator can have a database with load balancer telling

statement: Always reuse existing tools instead of re-implementing what other systems already implement.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why are you re-implementing things that are already implemented by other systems? Just reuse the stuff. Always.

statement: A student's answer 'connection pooling' as the tool for collecting metrics was dismissed by the teacher.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Connection pooling.
flags: check: probably the teacher calling on a student named Alok

statement: The vitals are metrics that should be logged, with scaling up and down done on the basis of those metrics; one student's team uses CloudWatch for this but scales manually, which the teacher accepted as the right kind of tool.
detail: Teacher: 'That's a good one. CloudWatch is that.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So we use CloudWatch based, but we are doing it manually.
flags: check: "Correct." at the end of Student 4's 01:34:55 turn may be the teacher's

statement: A telemetry agent is a process running on each host that emits the host's metrics (e.g. to CloudWatch or a metrics store).
detail: A student (Student 3) suggested 'CloudWatch or a telemetry agent'; another student asked what a telemetry agent is and where it is installed; Student 3 and the teacher answered.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: this is the telemetry agent that is running on the host, which is emitting metrics

statement: A student suggested the telemetry agent emit to some log storage with alarms on top; the teacher told the class not to go into alarms.
detail: Teacher: 'don't go into alarm' - the point is a generic central metrics store (next items).
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Probably some log storage. And then from there like we can have alarms or something.

statement: An organization building load balancers will anyway have a generic central place where key vitals and metrics of all machines are ingested, for example Prometheus.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you would anyway have a place where all these key vitals and metrics are getting ingested

statement: Prometheus is a brilliant tool that scales amazingly; see prometheus.io.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's a brilliant, brilliant, brilliant tool that scales amazingly.

statement: Do not limit the design to the system at hand (emit metrics to the orchestrator, store them in its DB); thinking realistically about the whole organization naturally leads to a cost-efficient solution.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Don't limit it. Think, if you think realistically you will automatically start to make sense into a very cost efficient solution

statement: Vitals of every VM, backend servers as well as LB servers, go to one central location so the orchestrator can decide to scale backend or LB servers; one place of ingestion and query solves the problem.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: having that one place of ingestion and query would solve the problem

statement: Telemetry agents on every VM (LB and backend) push data to Prometheus; the orchestrator periodically checks the average utilization there and decides whether to scale LB servers up or down or add backend servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let them push the data to Prometheus

statement: This is what AWS autoscaling groups / autoscaling policies do: you configure a rule like 'if average CPU utilization is this, do this', and internally they query a metrics store (their proprietary equivalent of Prometheus) and act when the condition is met.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So autoscaling group in AWS world or the autoscaling policies is just you configure.

statement: Multiple LB servers are opaque to users, so the orchestrator itself has to scale the LB servers up and down using the metrics.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is opaque to your users. You just don't know about multiple LB servers there.

statement: Instead of building something specific just for the load balancer, plug it into a generic system (e.g. Prometheus for metrics).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: instead of doing something specific, just for this load balancer, try to build a generic

statement: Recap of the design so far: low-level details, where to store the configuration, making updates reactive, health checks, an orchestrator that scales backend and LB servers, and telemetry from every machine into Prometheus that the orchestrator checks periodically.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We added the orchestrator to scale up backend servers and LB servers and whatnot.

statement: With two LB servers the client still only has one address: the TCP connection is made to an LB server, so how does the client reach the other LB servers?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: now you have two LB servers. Client has IP address of one of them. How will client make request to other LB servers?

statement: The answer is DNS: the load balancers are mapped in DNS servers, and DNS hands out one of the LB servers.
detail: Proposed by a student (Student 8); the teacher: 'DNS is the correct answer, but let's go detail into it.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: So we have a mapping of load balancers in DNS servers

statement: The DNS entry for a load balancer holds multiple machine IP addresses (e.g. 10.0.0.1, 10.0.0.2), not ports.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: will be multiple machine IP addresses, not just ports.

statement: A student argued that load balancers should be public and only internal servers private; the teacher corrected that not all load balancers are public.
detail: The teacher: a load balancer in front of a very critical internal microservice should not be public; and private load balancers cannot rely on a single LB server either ('What if that goes down?').
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: I think load balancers should be public and internal server should be private, right?

statement: A load balancer for a critical internal service should not be public; putting it in (public) DNS would seem to force it to be public, and a private LB still cannot be just one LB server because that could go down.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: imagine there is a very critical service that load balancer you

statement: Giving clients the IP address of the LB virtual machine does not scale: an IP address is fixed to a machine, two machines cannot share it, so the LB servers would not be scalable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because IP address is fixed to a machine, you cannot have two machines handling the same thing.

statement: A domain name abstracts multiple IP addresses; every load balancer you create gets its own domain name (e.g. payments.lb.google.com) behind which sit the IPs of its LB servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So what is something that abstracts multiple IP addresses? Domain name.

statement: Many people think DNS only means public DNS (google.com, facebook.com), but DNS can be private; the load balancer's domain is a private domain.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When someone talks about DNS, everyone just thinks about public DNS, google.com, facebook.com, right? But DNS can be private also.

statement: Work on an SRE team for at least a year and a half; it teaches things like private DNS that many engineers do not know.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I always recommend people to work on SRE teams at least for a year and a half at least

statement: You can launch your own DNS server; it is a very lightweight, simple process. CoreDNS is a good open-source DNS server, one of the most common simple implementations, used by the entire Kubernetes fraternity.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There is a nice, very good open source project called CoreDNS. The entire Kubernetes fraternity uses CoreDNS.

statement: A private CoreDNS instance runs inside your infrastructure, and every machine is configured to use it as its DNS address, so any domain name it looks up is resolved by CoreDNS.
detail: Look at how to configure CoreDNS to see this.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: on every machine, you specify this as your DNS address
flags: check: fragment "On each of your machine, as your loopback IP address." unclear

statement: Cloud providers such as AWS or GCP run a bunch of DNS servers, each with this kind of configuration.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So if you are AWS or GCP, there are a bunch of DNS servers running

statement: When a domain name has multiple IP addresses, the DNS server picks one using the same strategies as load balancing: round robin, weighted round robin and so on.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Round robin, weighted round robin, all of the strategies apply here as well.

statement: A DNS request for a load balancer's name resolves to one LB server IP, which is sent to the user; the user then connects to that IP and the normal load balancing flow takes over.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It resolves into an IP address. This IP address is sent to the user.

statement: If all requests routed through DNS, DNS would become a bottleneck and itself act like a load balancer; a student answered 'multiple DNS servers', which the teacher noted just moves the problem (load balancing between DNS servers).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: isn't all the requests routing through DNS not making DNS a bottleneck?

statement: A student described DNS as picking an LB IP and forwarding the request to that load balancer; the teacher corrected: then DNS would be the load balancer. DNS only sends the IP back to the client, and the client makes the request itself.
detail: After the correction the student answered: 'DNS should send the IP address to client back and then the client will make request.' Teacher: 'Correct.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: DNS according to its strategy will pick the IP address and send out that request to that particular load balancer.

statement: DNS is not a proxy: it is only a name resolution service that, given a human-readable name, returns an IP address - nothing more, nothing less.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: DNS is not a proxy. DNS is just someone who is resolving the IP address.

statement: The client always caches the resolved IP address for some time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Client always caches the resolved IP address for some time.

statement: Request flow: the client resolves the name via DNS, connects to the returned LB server, the LB server forwards to a backend server and returns the response; this is exactly what happens behind the scenes whenever you make an HTTP request.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is what when you make an HTTP request to anybody. This is exactly what happens behind the scenes.

statement: This is how the load balancer scales: when the orchestrator sees the need for a new LB server it spins one up and adds its IP (e.g. 10.0.0.3) to the load balancer's DNS entry.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it spin up an LB server and updated the DNS entry for that

statement: Final design: multiple LB servers, an orchestrator, the configuration database, an LB console where developers make changes, and a Prometheus server receiving periodic vitals (CPU, memory, disk) from all servers; the orchestrator periodically queries Prometheus and, when LB servers need to scale, scales them and makes an entry in the CoreDNS server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Orchestrator periodically queries Prometheus to see if LB server needs to scale up or not.

statement: The client of a load balancer is not just an end user; it can be another microservice or server - anything that resolves a human-readable name.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it can be another microservice also, server also, user also, anything
flags: unclear: "all that drawing user i can"

statement: Final request path: the name (e.g. lb.payments.google.com) is resolved by CoreDNS, the client connects to the returned LB server, the LB server picks a backend by its balancing strategy, the backend processes and the response goes back to the user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: request goes to CoreDNS, gets it back, gets the IP address, it connects to the LB server

statement: Final config path: any alteration (a failed health check, autoscaling, a developer change) updates the configuration DB; CDC, the LB server or the orchestrator pushes a message to the Redis broker, a real-time Pub/Sub that sends it to all LB servers, which update their in-memory copy of the configuration.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because this is a real time Pub/Sub, it is real time, in real time sent to all the LB servers.

statement: Using the real-time Pub/Sub broker guarantees message delivery of configuration changes to all LB servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now this is what happens is you guarantee message delivery because of this.

statement: Because each LB server works from an in-memory copy of the configuration updated by push, load balancing loses no performance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This way you do not lose on the performance while you do your entire load balancing.

statement: Further reading: the Maglev paper, 'a fast and reliable software load balancer' - easy, not difficult at all, one of the first papers the teacher read; it gives more granular details of what was covered.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Maglev, a fast and reliable software load balancer. It's really easy.

statement: The load balancer part covered an extreme low-level implementation and a high-level design; some pieces floating around are sneak peeks of what comes in future weeks, and locks are covered after the break.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we covered an extreme low level implementation of load balancer, a high level design of load balancer

statement: If a client's cached DNS entry points to an LB server that has gone down, the client does not wait for the TTL: when it cannot connect it immediately invalidates its cache and asks CoreDNS for another IP address - a reactive approach.
detail: Student 2 asked about a local DNS cache with a TTL making the site unavailable until the TTL expires.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: I would explicitly invalidate my cache and make a call to CoreDNS

statement: Reacting to a failed connection is like a toothache: you do not wait for your periodic dentist visit when it hurts, you go immediately.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You'd say no, I'll only visit a dentist only when the time comes. But if it's hurting, will you not go there?

statement: CoreDNS is not a single point of failure: you run multiple CoreDNS servers.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: You have multiple CoreDNS servers running.

statement: To find which CoreDNS server to reach you have a DNS for CoreDNS; recursively, at some level the load becomes so small that one server handles it - one single point of failure with a standby node, the base condition of the recursion.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: So there is one single point of failure still in a system, which has a standby node. That's the base condition of the recursive.

statement: Of the many levels on a path (traceroute to google.com can show around 21), every level is horizontally scalable except one tiny single point of failure with a standby node, which rarely goes down and is replaced by the standby within seconds.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: And every single one of them is horizontally scalable, except one, which is single point of failure with a standby node.

statement: External end users resolve names through the public DNS configured in their OS (e.g. Route 53), not through a private CoreDNS.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: It goes to public DNS server and not a private DNS server.

statement: If a load balancer serves external users it is public: then the private CoreDNS does not come into the picture and resolution is a public DNS resolution.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If you're making it public, then this does not come into picture.

statement: For public load balancers, adding LB servers 'kind of' updates public DNS, but there is an intermediate proxy layer in between; resolution happens across several layers and every LB server still has a domain name, just not necessarily public. The details are proprietary; the Maglev paper explains more.
detail: The teacher kept it simple on purpose and offered to answer in coming weeks after students read Maglev.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: think of it like kind of that there is one intermediate proxy layer that sits in between that takes care of that

statement: A load balancer balances across a homogeneous set of servers; it is not an API gateway. Each service has its own load balancer with its own LB servers and its own CoreDNS entries.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: It's balancing across homogeneous set of servers. Right. This is not an API gateway.

statement: After the break the class covers remote locks and distributed locks; the teacher would not compromise on depth even if the session stretched.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Remote locks and distributed locks.

statement: Remote and distributed locks are among the most important things in distributed systems because they ensure the correctness and consistency of data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's the one that ensures, as I said, ensures the correctness and consistency of data

statement: A lock manager is a remote machine that keeps track of which item is locked by which machine, so it can coordinate (e.g. refuse an operation on an item that is locked).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: lock manager is a remote machine that acts as a lock manager which keeps track, hey, which item is locked by which machine

statement: In the airline check-in system rows were locked exclusively and the database kept in memory which transaction held each lock - everything in one machine and process; with multiple machines that must coordinate you need a remote lock manager.
case_study: Airline check-in system from an earlier session (exclusive row locks).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So that is why you need to have a remote lock manager that does that.

statement: Threads synchronize through in-memory constructs - mutex, semaphore, explicit locking, atomic instructions - because what is common between threads is RAM; each database transaction in the airline check-in system is a thread.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because multiple threads synchronizes through an in-memory thing. Mutex, semaphore, explicit locking, atomic instructions, whatnot.

statement: Around 2008-2009, in first year of college, the teacher ran apt-get upgrade in two terminals on Ubuntu hoping it would be twice as fast; the second one failed saying the dpkg.lock file exists, so multiple instances could not run.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the other used to say dpkg.lock file exists. We cannot move forward.

statement: apt-get synchronizes processes through the disk: at most one apt-get upgrade may run (two would leave an inconsistent state), so on start a process checks for the dpkg.lock file - if it exists the process kills itself, otherwise it creates it, proceeds, and deletes the file when done.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When the process starts, it creates a dpkg.lock file.
flags: asr: [?at the same time | asr: "at the center"]

statement: Synchronization uses the closest shared storage: threads synchronize through memory, processes through disk (the closest storage shared between processes), and machines through the network - which is where remote locks come in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Multiple processes synchronize through disk because that is the closest storage which is shared between processes.

statement: What is shared between multiple machines is not disk but the network, so machines synchronize using remote locks over the network.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now when you think about multiple machines, what is shared between them? Disk? No. Network.

statement: Practical examples beat theory any day.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: practical beats theory any day

statement: Hypothetical: a badly built remote queue gives zero protection - its API just does queue.pop, which is not thread safe, so consumers firing at the same time may get the same message.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: queue.pop is not thread safe.

statement: Requirement for the hypothetical queue (id queue 7, remote like SQS but without SQS's guarantees): three consumers, and at any given time only one consumer may read from it - exclusivity; throughput does not matter.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: at any given point in time, only one consumer is allowed to read from the queue
flags: check: words may be missing here (02:10:37)

statement: A synchronized block around the queue's get/pop does not work: the queue is remote and the consumers run on different machines.
detail: Teacher: 'that's remote. This queue is remote. This is not local queue.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: we can have like a synchronized block when the get or pop method is being used

statement: Taking a lock on the server where the queue runs is not possible: the queue is a black box and you cannot change it or access its server.
detail: Student 4 proposed a lock where the queue is implemented; the teacher: 'You cannot change queue. Queue is black box for you.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: the consumer needs to first get the lock and before accessing the queue

statement: Adding an intermediate layer in front of the queue that lets one request through at a time was rejected: it just adds one more layer, while the goal is to implement a lock manager.
detail: Teacher: 'then that layer becomes a portal [as heard]. You have queue already. Now you're adding one more layer to that.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: Maybe we can introduce a layer in between.

statement: Running another process on the queue's machine is not possible either: for the consumers the queue is a black box exposing a single unprotected API call.
detail: Student 7 asked whether the lock could be another process on the queue's machine; the teacher: 'No, you cannot. That's a black box for you... you get message from the queue, but that is unprotected.'
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: That's a black box for you. That's a remote call for you.

statement: Use a database as the lock manager: store a key for the resource (e.g. Q7) whose value is the consumer currently allowed to read; that consumer reads, others see another name there and do not read.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So what you do, you use a database as a lock manager.

statement: When the lock holder finishes it removes its name; the other consumers then compete to put their name in, and the winner reads while the rest wait.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now consumer two and consumer three would compete who puts their name inside this.

statement: A classic lock manager stores exactly two things: what the resource is and who owns it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is exactly what you need to store, that what's the resource and who owns this resource

statement: If a consumer takes the lock and dies before deleting it, the lock is held perpetually; so every lock entry needs a TTL - automatic expiration that deletes it if it was not deleted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: for everything we need a TTL, automatic expiration

statement: The lock store must offer key-value access, atomic instructions and TTL; Redis gives all three, which is why the most common remote lock implementation is the Redis-based Redlock.
detail: At 02:16:05 the requirements are listed as 'key value-based access, instructions and TTL'; at 02:18:46 as 'atomic instructions and automatic expirations'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: which database gives you all three Redis, which is why you see the most common remote locking implementation is Redis based implementation called Redlock

statement: Because the black-box queue gives no protection and all we have is its network interface, we must implement the protection we need ourselves - hence the remote lock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We have to implement the protection that we need.

statement: Each consumer's code acquires the lock, reads the message and releases the lock; all consumers keep calling Redis to acquire it, one succeeds and reads while the others wait, and when it releases the next one gets in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you would acquire the lock, read the message and then release the lock

statement: In Redis the lock entry says: this resource is owned by this consumer right now, with an expiration of 5 minutes; if the owner does not delete it within 5 minutes it expires automatically, so no lock is held forever.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This consumer owns this resource at this very moment with an expiration of 5 minutes.

statement: Acquire-lock code: the consumer knows its own ID (e.g. IP address or host name) and, in a while-true loop, tries to SET the lock key (Q7) with its ID using SET NX with an expiration of 300 seconds.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I am not just doing normal set, I am doing set nx.

statement: Redis SET NX sets a key only if it does not already exist (here with an expiration); it returns 1 if it set the key and 0 if not, so an existing lock is never overwritten.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis gives you that command out of the box, which says set nx, that set only when it is non-existent.

statement: Every Redis command is atomic: while one command executes no other command runs on Redis, so of many consumers trying at the same time only one succeeds - the property the lock relies on.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this command of Redis is an atomic command, which means that when one, this command is executing, no other command would ever execute on Redis

statement: If SET NX succeeds the consumer owns the lock, exits the loop and reads the message from the queue; otherwise it keeps looping until someone releases the lock, so most consumers spin in the while loop.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So you continue this while loop forever, forever as in unless someone releases it.

statement: Releasing the lock by simply deleting the key is wrong: a process could delete the key from Redis even though it does not own the lock at that moment.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it is possible for a process to delete the key from Redis even though it does not own the lock at the moment

statement: Timeout edge case: consumer 1 holds the lock with a 5-minute expiry; it takes too long, Redis deletes the key, consumer 2 acquires the lock, then consumer 1 reaches its release and deletes the lock now owned by consumer 2.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So consumer 1 is actually deleting the lock which is owned by consumer 2. This is the edge case.

statement: Never delete a lock that is not yours: on release, get the current owner and delete only if it is you.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you cannot delete in case the lock is not yours

statement: Even the get-then-delete check fails in normal client code: after you see you own the lock and before you delete, the key can expire and consumer 2 acquire it, so you delete consumer 2's lock.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But after this, the expiration kicked in. The key got evicted. Consumer two own the lock. And then you deleted.

statement: Edge cases like this are where distributed systems show their 'glory': if you miss one, your system is not correct.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your system is not correct if you are missing out on this edge case

statement: Make the check-and-delete atomic with Redis EVAL: write it as a Lua script that Redis runs in one shot; while it runs Redis does nothing else, so nobody can acquire the lock in between - a kind of transaction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in which you don't write this as Python code, but a Lua script, which you run in one shot on Redis

statement: When designing distributed systems, imagine that after every single line something lags or goes down, and check that the system still works; go to that granularity rather than just saying 'I'll have a lock'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Imagine after every single line, something lag is coming, something's going down, something's happening. See if your system still functions well.

statement: A single Redis lock instance is not fault tolerant: if it goes down nobody can acquire the lock and the whole system stalls - a single point of failure.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Because if this goes down, their entire system is done, because no one can acquire the lock.

statement: Very few companies use distributed locks; most startups never need them because the cloud provides those guarantees, but if you work at AWS or GCP building those services you must handle it yourself (Chubby is a great example).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Very few companies use distributed locks. Most startups never think of using distributed locks because cloud provides you those guarantees.

statement: Distributed locks exist only to solve the single point of failure problem of single-instance lock systems; it is not enough to say 'run it in a cluster'. The teacher has seen and used them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: distributed locks come in places where you want to avoid the single point of failure problem of single lock instances

statement: Distributed lock acquisition: run several (e.g. five) fully independent Redis servers - no multi-master replication - and try to acquire the lock on all of them, sequentially or in parallel.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: instead of taking lock on one Redis, you take locks on multiple Redis servers

statement: You own the distributed lock only if you acquired it on more than 50% of the nodes (e.g. 3 of 5); holding the majority means no other contending process can also hold it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you succeed in acquiring lock on more than 50 percent of nodes

statement: If you fail to get the majority, immediately release the locks you did get so other processes can contend; processes keep retrying and someone eventually wins and processes the message.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you will immediately release the lock on these two, and so that let other process

statement: Distributed locks take a toll on performance and throughput, so they are not used in high-throughput systems; they are used where a high degree of correctness and fault tolerance is required.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It is typically used in systems that demand high degree of correctness.

statement: Because the lock is distributed, one Redis node going down is no problem; edge cases remain (e.g. instances holding the lock going down afterwards) that still affect correctness, but the probability is reduced to a bare minimum.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there are still edge cases, there is still problem with correctness in it, but still reduces the probability of hitting that to a bare minimum
flags: asr: [?an edge case | asr: "in each case"]

statement: The idea of distributed systems: take a single node of X and make it distributed; every single piece of your architecture needs to be horizontally scalable like this.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every single piece in your architecture needs to be horizontally scalable like this.

statement: Further reading: Google's Chubby paper, a lock service for loosely coupled distributed systems, still used in Google production; the first research paper the teacher read (as an assignment); very influential.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Chubby, read this paper. This is what Google still uses in production.

statement: Further reading: Martin Kleppmann's blog on why you should not use Redlock - a rare edge case where it does not work; recommended.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Martin Kleppmann has a blog written on it that why you should not use Redlock.

verbatim: And I have three or four videos on my channel on distributed transactions.

statement: Distributing the lock does not handle scale - it reduces throughput; what it gains is fault tolerance and higher availability.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Here we distributed this part not to handle scale. Did we? No. It is reducing the scale. It is reducing the throughput.

statement: Two different patterns: scaling horizontally to handle scale versus making something distributed to get fault tolerance, reliability and availability - which is why the teacher uses different phrases for them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are either scaling it horizontally to handle scale or you are making it distributed.
